references.text: The context 'after these things' refers back to Abram's victory over the kings and his meeting with Melchizedek, which is the immediate background for God's assurance in Gen 15:1.
The Lord's original promise to Abram to make him a great nation and bless him forms the basis for the promise of great reward in Gen 15:1.
God says 'do not fear' to Isaac and promises to bless him for Abraham's sake, which directly mirrors the words spoken to Abram in Gen 15:1.
Israel is called blessed because the Lord is their shield and help, a direct parallel to God's promise to be Abram's shield.
David expresses trust in the Lord as his shield, reflecting God's assurance to Abram that He would be his shield.
David calls the Lord his rock, fortress, and shield, a parallel to God's promise of protection to Abram.
The Lord is described as sun and shield who gives grace and glory, reflecting the promise of protection and reward given to Abram.
Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the Lord are encouraged to trust in Him as their help and shield.
The psalmist calls the Lord his refuge and shield, and places his hope in His word.
The Lord is a shield for those who walk in righteousness, a parallel to God's promise to be Abram's shield.
God assures Israel not to fear, for He is with them and will strengthen and help them—parallel to 'do not fear, Abram' in Gen 15:1.
Without faith it is impossible to please God, for whoever comes to Him must believe that He exists and rewards those who seek Him—the promise 'your reward shall be very great' is reflected here.
The promise of 'great reward' in Gen 15:1 unfolds concretely as a multitude of nations and a name change in Gen 17:5.
Gen 15:1 highlights God's side of the covenant (protection and reward), while Gen 17:9 emphasizes humanity's side (the duty to keep the covenant).
The divine exhortation 'Do not fear' in Gen 15:1 is found again in the NT (Mark 6:50) as a constant comfort from God in human fear.
Both verses use "reward" as a central motif of God's righteous recompense and restoration, even though the contexts (Abram versus Rachel) differ.
